Mr. Speaker, we understand that some progress has been made as far as negotiations are concerned. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will rise in his place and give us some indication of whether or not government employees who have grievances in the established process are satisfied, so that we will be in a position to pass the Bill with some assurance that the employees have reached a satisfactory agreement.
The particular motion before the House has been adequately discussed, so I will not go into the need for the extension of time. If the Parliamentary Secretary can give us those assurances there will be no need at all for this kind of a motion. The procedures followed in this Bill have been very bad, and before we have any other divestitures or privatizations we should be discussing procedures.
I would like to put before the Government, and possibly 1 will during third reading, the kinds of concerns the people of Canada, the employees affected and the business community have about the procedures used by the Government, procedures which are not necessarily for the good of the employees or for the good of Canada, but are based on an ideology the Government has accepted and is pushing through without any particular concern for the people involved. If the Government insists on doing that, it would be necessary to have a procedure which would allow the people involved to know that all of the information is before them and that they have had an opportunity to protect themselves and Canadians as a whole.
In every case that we have had of a formation of a Crown corporation the reason for the formation was well established. Public interest required it and in most of them we passed a Bill in this House to make sure the public interest was served by the formation of such a Crown corporation.
It is incredible, after a long and basic discussion to establish a corporation, to find that suddenly the Government can sell it and ask Parliament to rubber stamp the procedure after the sale is finalized. The Government has made the sale with such little information available to the public, to the employees and to Parliament that nobody really knows what is going on. We have had three cases of Crown corporation divestitures. In each case the amount of information available to Parliament, to the people and to the employees has been inadequate, and concern for the employees has been inadequate.
Even as we now discuss report stage and this amendment which asks to defer the process, the real concern is whether the Government is ready to establish the kind of procedures which would avoid the anguish these employees felt when they found themselves being pawned off. due as long-standing and loyal employees of a government corporation and members of the Public Service Alliance.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for controlling this unruly crowd.
Before I was interrupted by the mass exodus of those who were here to help us get through report stage of the Bill, I was about to delineate the agreement and to discuss its main points, as requested by my colleague from the New Democratic Party.
Our main concern in the second reading debate and committee stage was that of the employees' pension. I am pleased to say that through input from the committee and Hon. Members from all Parties, the employees of Canadian Arsenals Limited and the Government of Canada, through Treasury Board, have reached an agreement. Treasury Board has confirmed this agreement by letter. SNC has agreed and has accepted the agreement. Perhaps I could be offered the opportunity of informing my colleagues in the House of what the decision was, if they have not already been so advised. It
involves a transfer to each member who so elects the actuarial value, with a minimum equal to twice the members' contributions with interest, of the pension accrued at the date of privatization. That is on an ongoing basis.
Under the Public Service Superannuation Act and the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act, in a defined contribution plan, a money purchase plan, the actuarial value being based on the actuarial assumptions used by the chief actuary in his report on the valuation of the plan as of December 31, 1980, SNC should treat these contributions as vested in the name of each member, and those members who are presently buying past services will be given the option to carry on.
I feel this is a tremendous move. I would like to personally thank my colleagues in the Liberal, New Democratic and Conservative Parties who spent those hours in committee and in the deliberations behind the committee. It is very difficult for the Government to dictate to private sector employers how they will treat their new employees, but we are very pleased that through the recommendations by all three Parties and Members thereof a behind-the-scenes agreement was reached with the Government of Canada and Crown employees, and that SNC has ratified that agreement, all parties are now satisfied. Again, I would like to thank all Hon. Members for their participation in this very worthwhile debate.

Mr. Speaker, I think the debate on Bill C-87 has gone on far too long, for the simple reason that from the outset the Government should have proceeded differently. We were not satisfied with the way the Government decided to sell the corporation while providing very little protection for its employees. We have spoken at length about this Bill, not because we object to the principle of privatization or because we object to the sale of Canadian Arsenals Ltd. in particular. On the contrary, we think that manufacturing munitions is not an area in which the State should be involved. Nor do we have any difficulty with the prospective buyer, SNC, which is entirely responsible and which we hope will be able to run this company so that it makes a profit and also in a manner that is considerate of its employees.
However, as we said in the House last week, and more specifically last Friday, we realized that employees at Canadian Arsenals Ltd. were getting very little protection under this Bill. Earlier in the debate, there was a reference to a study made at the Government's request by a number of consultants, a study the Government refused to release, and that is why our party was for some time very much against giving Bill C-87 speedy passage through the House, and that is also why my colleague, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott- Russell (Mr. Boudria) spoke several times in the House and, in fact, spearheaded an attack to have the Bill amended. And we are surprised that Conservative Members from Quebec did not rise in the House to defend Canadian Arsenals employees.
April 24, 1986

Mr. Speaker, the first draft introduced by the Government was more or less a package deal to sell the captive employees along with the corporation - 450 or close to 450 employees at the Le Gardeur plant and about 50 more at Saint-Augustin in the riding of Portneuf. However, some amendments were made and we are now prepared to support the Bill. We would have been quite concerned had the sale been concluded without guaranteeing more employee protection, for it might have created a dangerous precedent now that the Government is intent on selling other Crown corporations to private interests. We wanted to avoid such a precedent. As a matter of fact we are somewhat surprised that the Government's first version of this Bill should have been an attempt to take CAL employees for a ride.
Be that as it may, I want to say that our victory does not leave a bitter taste. As Liberals we feel that we have played a leading role in changing this Bill. As I mentioned earlier, we took this initiative under the guidance of my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell and we are pleased with the outcome of this matter.
I want to commend the Public Service Alliance for leading the fight on behalf of its membership, particularly Mr. Jean Bergeron. I also extend congratulations to the buyer, the SNC firm, for being so patient during the many weeks it took to get the Bill through the Commons. In all honesty, the Government deserves praise for finally seeing the light and introducing amendments which CAL employees and Opposition Parties can live with. The ultimate result is that all Members of the House are now prepared to pass this measure. It goes to prove that constructive debate can indeed make Members of different political persuasions see eye to eye. Again I applaud Government Members for showing flexibility in this instance. Hopefully this will be a precedent, in the sense that if ever the Governent wants to sell other Crown corporations to the private sector the sale terms will provide adequate protection for the transferred employees.
That is all I wanted to say, Mr. Speaker, and I hope the Bill will get swift third reading passage today.

Mr. Speaker, this debate is on third reading of Bill C-87 which deals with the privatization of Canadians Arsenals Limited and its sale to SNC Group of Quebec. A number of points have been raised during the course of the debate with respect to the general questions of privatization.
In opening my remarks I would like to say that it has taken a long time to carry out this sale. One of the major reasons being that the Government did not think through exactly what it intended to do. Because of the program of privatization it is a sale which has been driven by ideology as opposed to common sense. I say this because the figures we have indicate that Canadian Arsenals is an extremely profitable company and its profitability was rapidly rising. Of course, it is in a
Canadian Arsenals Limited
managed market, in the sense that most of its sales have to be to the Government of Canada for defence purposes. Therefore, its profitability has to do with the prices paid by the Department of National Defence for munitions and other goods it buys from this firm. Nonetheless, it had to have a substantial amount of efficiency. It was being run effectively since it achieved such a profit turn-around and has shown dramatic improvements in profits over the last few years. If it was so good, and if it was making a contribution to the people of Canada in terms of money coming back, then why sell it? Why not look at other alternatives?
Canadian Arsenals has indicated that it has a fairly major re-equipment and investment program to carry out. Under those circumstances the rigidity of the Government has been in not understanding that Crown corporations should have commercial freedom to do such things as raising money privately, if it is not available through the Treasury. That is stupid. It seems to me that it is an ideological decision. The Government, in being conservative, wants to prove that public enterprise does not work. Therefore, it hamstrings public enterprises in various ways. It makes it difficult for public enterprises to work effectively by such measures as denying them access to capital in the market if they cannot obtain it through the Department of Finance or through the Treasury.
I am suggesting that what the SNC Group intends to do in terms of future development of Canadian Arsenals could just as easily have been done in public hands. I know that SNC is looking at the possibility of exploring export markets for Canadian Arsenals. It has said that CAL was not very vigorous in this area.
I believe there is a moral question here in terms of what export markets we will see. I for one do not want to see Canadian Arsenals in private hands selling to racist regimes such as South Africa, or selling into the hot spots around the world where there are shooting wars going on, or selling to dictators such as General Pinochet of Chile. I do not care whether the company is in public or private hands. As Canadians we share the view that there ought to be some fairly substantial regulation of where munitions being produced in Canada are sold. What is the restraint on Canadian Arsenals from selling to the Americans or to our NATO allies? I think the restraint, if it existed, has been largely a self-imposed restraint. After all, the Royal Canadian Mint sells its services in terms of coinage to many countries in and outside the Commonwealth. I believe it sells to some 20 or 30 countries. It has developed a thriving export market. Therefore, there is no reason, in principle, why CAL could not have done the same thing while it was under public ownership.
We will not resolve all the questions concerning privatization now. However, the Government seems to have the view of "heads you lose and tails we win". If a Crown corporation is having difficulties, or losing money, the Government says: "Look, it's a loser. Let's get rid of it". If a Crown corporation, such as this one, is making money, it says: "Look, it's making money. Let's get rid of it". There do not seem to be any

Mr. Speaker, the mandate for a company such as Canadian Arsenals could tend to become lost because it has been a Crown corporation for so long. I do not think the former or the present Governments have understood that these mandates have to be reviewed. It is not understood that there has to be some real accountability and thinking in terms of who sits on the boards of Crown corporations and what kind of responsibilities they will fulfil. It is not just an ordinary private corporation. Nor is it an instrument of Government. It is something in between. Canadians have not done too badly in terms of development in that intermediate area. However, we tend to lose the thread from time to time. The Government's practice of saying that it does not understand what it is all about and, therefore, it will get rid of it, is not the best solution.
During the course of debate we raised a number of specific issues concerning job security, pensions and the recognition of union rights under various labour codes. I suggest that before any other privatizations take place involving a change in labour jurisdiction the Government should ensure that the question of successor rights is hammered out before hand and not after, as was the case in this particular circumstance. In this circumstance, technically, the workers could wind up with no union, or another union after the switch is made to Quebec
labour jurisdiction. I am sure that the Public Service Alliance has been doing some work to try to ensure that it can continue to represent the workers, something which it has done for many years.
In the private sector under Ontario legislation, for example, there is the concept of successor rights. When selling a company, new management cannot evade the responsibility of adhering to the contract which the employees had with the previous mangement. The concept of successor rights does not mean that the union which happens to be there has the right to be there forever, because there are processes of decertification. This being a free society, I am sure the Alliance would accept, as would any other union, that that should continue to be a potential recourse for employees who decide they do not want to have a union or want to change the union which they have. Sometimes it is necessary because the union loses the track itself and is no longer effective in defending its members, or it becomes like certain unions which no longer really work in the true interests of its members.
However, it seems to me that at least there should have been an agreement between the Canada authorities and the Quebec provincial authorities which would have provided de facto successor rights in this particular case and, therefore, bridged the transition from federal labour code jurisdiction to provincial. I call upon the Government to ensure that that occurs in the future. I should now like to turn to the issue of pensions.

I gather the Government has learned a few lessons concerning the pension entitlement of Canadian Arsenals Ltd. employees who were participants in the Canada Government Pension Plan and who will now have the option either of transferring their pension contributions into SNC's plan or keeping their entitlement until the date of sale in the Government of Canada Pension Plan.
That is not the best of solutions, but it is much better than the situation that was provided for before the amendment we just supported was introduced.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest the reason why our Party supported Amendment No. 3 moved by the Minister, and which we just voted on, was specifically that we are now satisfied, after contacting our friends in the Public Service Alliance, that the pension problem of those employees is now adequately solved.
It is not an ideal solution, but it seems the union representing the employees is satisfied that it is the best available to protect those 800 employees' vested interest with respect to their pensions.
Mr. Speaker, I am quite pleased that the work done by my friend the Hon. Member for Price Albert (Mr. Hovdebo), the Members of the New Democratic Party and of the Liberal Party and our representations and our insisting on the matter
April 24, 1986

of the pension entitlement of those 800 employees have finally led to an acceptable solution for the employees concerned.
It seems that employees who elect to retain their pension entitlement in the Public Service pension system, will not only qualify for their pensions, but that their years of service with the new owners, SNC Corporation, will be taken into account when determining their pension entitlement. It seems that the existing indexation that covers the Public Service Pension Plan will carry over for those employees.
Unfortunately, this will not apply to that portion of their employment that will continue with the new owners. However, indexation on 20, 25 or 30 years of service, according to the situation of a number of employees, will apply.
I am therefore quite pleased that Parliament, through its efforts, has succeded in convincing the Minister, and perhaps the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Mclnnes), the actual owner of the Canadian Arsenals Ltd. Corporation, of what the problem was. Perhaps it was Treasury Board, or perhaps even Government officials who did not realize how important it was to be flexible on such an issue.

I will say in English as well that I am pleased a solution of the pension issue which is satisfactory to the employees has been finally reached. We understand and they understand that it is not ideal but, nonetheless, it goes a long way toward achieving the goals they set out at the beginning. Certainly it goes an awful lot further than shoving people off into the private sector, giving them back their contributions, and basically not an awful lot more, after years of contributing to the pension plan of the Government of Canada and expecting to receive a decent pension plan as one of the conditions or benefits of staying with that particular employer, rather than moving to an available job down the street or in another community which might be more attractive or have a weekly wage that is perhaps a bit more attractive. I am glad that has been achieved. As I said in French, I think in large measure it is due to the efforts of the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo), our caucus and that of the Liberals. I see the Parliamentary Secretary encouraging me as I say that. I would say to him that I am glad he dealt with the matters seriously and worked hard to try to find a solution.
I suspect that one of the problems within Government was that the Treasury Board, being responsible for the Public Service superannuation plan, was being rather sticky and difficult to deal with. I will not describe the expression on the Parliamentary Secretary's face as I make that comment; it would be indiscreet for me to do so. However, I say generally to the Government that in these matters of privatization, the Macdonald Commission talked about the need for more flexibility in how we run our affairs. For goodness sake, that has to begin with the Government of Canada. We have to show some example.
Because many things are happening in mixed areas of the economy, because activities which were public are becoming
Canadian Arsenals Limited
private, like airport security activities that were privatized and are now coming back into the public sector, we must be realistic in understanding that we should be trying to accommodate to the best of our capacity the legitimate needs and desires of people in these cases. Treasury Board should not be digging in its heels and suggesting that it is a lovely idea but that it cannot be done because it has never been done before. We have not before had a Government with 211 seats. Many of the things which the Government has done have never been done before. In some cases it is unfortunate that they are being done now. However, I suggest that rules and regulations in terms of what occurred in the Government of Canada in the past should not impede necessary arrangements when it comes to such things as dealing fairly with people who completely, unwittingly and beyond their control are affected by the Government's ideological decision on privatization in this particular case.
While I am happy that a solution has been reached, I am sorry it took so much effort on the part of people who had to negotiate and struggle in order to obtain a solution. If the Parliamentary Secretary and his Minister would like to join forces with people in our caucus in the future in order to overcome the ingrained resistance and conservatism of the Treasury Board and certain other central agencies within the Government of Canada, and if we can achieve some desirable results, we will be happy to do so. On the other hand, if the Parliamentary Secretary and his Minister would like to join forces with people in our Party in turning back this pressure for privatization, this ideological obsession with privatization, we would be happy to do that as well.
Mir. Hovdebo: Mr. Speaker, would the Hon. Member take a few moments to express the concerns of the union on a couple of other points? I refer firstly to the fact that employees were unable to continue in the plan they had, and secondly, to the hiatus which appears in the transfer between jurisdictions and the possibility of grievances during that period.

Even after that recognition is granted, there is still the period of time when the parties may be working out a new contract. There could be a lengthy period of time, not because of bad faith on either side, but because of the practical difficulties in doing something which has not been done before. This is why I am suggesting that there should have been a direct agreement between the Government of Canada and the Quebec Government over the question of how successor rights would be achieved.

April 24, 1986
Canadian Arsenals Limited
In general, SNC is acting in good faith. It is biting off a fair amount here because the turnover of Canadian Arsenals is not that far short of what was SNC's total turnover just a year or two ago. It is a major acquisition for SNC, but it seems to be going into it with a constructive spirit. The Government of Canada could have had SNC bind itself legally to the Government of Canada in the Agreement of Sale. SNC could not reach a legal agreement with the union, but this would have had no accreditation in legal terms after the sale until recognition was granted. Secondly, during that transition period I think that SNC should also have been required by the Government of Canada to agree that in the event of dispute there would then be an agreed upon means by which arbitration could be resorted to where matters could not be resolved otherwise.
I would remind the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Mclnnes), who is responsible for the Bill, that for some lengthy period of time the union was not able to meet with SNC. I suggested that that be done early when I met with the SNC representatives. They did not see the purchase agreement or the agreement in principle until the matter went to the legislative committee, and that was too late, Mr. Speaker. I am glad it occurred eventually but, as we found in the case of de Havil-land, there is no need to guard that information.
I was at a conference of public managers the other day where one of the workshops was on the theme of "consult with the public but don't tell them anything". speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I have spoken in this debate on several occasions and now I shall, if I may, add some further comments on this Bill. My hon. colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), who is out of town today on parliamentary business, has asked me to make a few comments on his behalf regarding Bill C-87 and the privatization of the Crown corporation Canadian Arsenals Ltd. by its sale to SNC.
Mr. Speaker, we know that the Government elected in 1984 wanted to meet its commitment to privatizing of certain companies, and had even suggested privatizing a considerable number of Crown corporations.
I think if we look back, we can see what the privatization policy has achieved, and wonder how it has worked, and in this
particular case, the sale of Canadian Arsenals Ltd., whether the exercise has been a successful and a beneficial one for Canadians. And that will be the main thrust of my comments.
Mr. Speaker, we know that since the privatization policy was announced, a secretariat was set up at Treasury Board, headed by Mr. Basil Beneteau, former Vice-President of the Board of Directors of Northern Telecom. His assistant is Mr. Lawrence J. O'Toole, previously federal co-ordinator of economic development in Ontario. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) selected Salomon Brothers as financial advises to the task force. So we have a privatization secretariat, and I imagine it is busy applying the criteria the Government has established, that is, how to privatize, what to privatize and under what conditions.
To date, Mr. Speaker, the Northern Transportation Company has been privatized, as well as de Havilland. The operation was less successful in the latter case because the de Havilland-Boeing transaction was somewhat confused and difficult. We even had to hold a special debate on it here in the House, and I think that this gave the Government the opportunity to learn something about privatization. There was of course the sales of Fisheries Canada, a sea product processing company in the Gaspe area, for an amount of $5 million, and the most recent case is the one now before us which concerns the divestiture of the Canadian Arsenals Limited Corporation to SNC.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, at the second reading stage, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell repeatedly asked two questions, with our support. One was: Did the Government consult the employees of Canadian Arsenals Limited before acting to privatize the corporation?
The second question we asked was this: If so, what was the result of this consultation and what are the concerns of the employees?
We knew from the unions and the employees themselves that the employees had not been consulted and that they were worried about such matters as their pension fund, and what the future held for them with the company which was to purchase Canadian Arsenals Limited.
Mr. Speaker, we then asked the Government to provide us with a report prepared by Arthur Andersen which the Government itself had requested and which apparently contained details of the transaction, but our request was rejected.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I remember having made speeches in the House on second reading to tell the Government: Listen, without the important information and data which we need concerning the consultations as well as the validity of the privatization and the benefits of this sale for Canadians, and because we are concerned about the working conditions and transfer of the company to the private sector, we want to see the famous Arthur Andersen report and we want to know what the conditions are concerning the employee's pension plans and the transfer of their jobs from the public sector to the private sector.
April 24, 1986

We spent a long time at second reading, Mr. Speaker, as you know, on this request in order to finally obtain from the Government the commitment that they would make public finally, at the report stage, the famous Arthur Andersen report. Then we moved from second reading stage to the committee stage. Finally, the Government made the Arthur Andersen report public, so that we realized, together with the Government, that improvements were required to the pension fund. Those are the problems which were addressed in committee and settled, I think, for the benefit of the Government, the SNC purchaser, but above all the benefit of employees who were seeking guarantees concerning their pension fund, its transfer to the public sector and many questions still unanswered concerning their benefits, their pensions, the indexation of these pensions, the future of their jobs, and especially their careers with the SNC.
I think that the Government has made an effort and I want to congratulate the Minister and the Parliamentary Secretary for listening to the requests of both the employees and the Official Opposition with the assistance of the New Democratic Party.
I think we should realize that Canadian Arsenals Ltd. is a company which five or six years ago managed to overcome serious problems with the help of its workers and has now become a profitable concern. Now, we wanted to get the cooperation of both employees and management, since they are the parties concerned, to come up with a solution that was equitable and fair, considering the employees' very reasonable demands concerning the conditions for transferring their pension fund contributions and also concerning their careers and their future with SNC.
Mr. Speaker, we do not object to privatization as such. The concept is aimed at letting the private sector take over activities that were controlled by the State. This can be done, as we know, either by selling the Government's shares or the corporation, or by the government simply getting out of the activities it was or is involved in.
Mr. Speaker, two words are foremost in my mind, and we hear them very often today: deregulation and privatization. Today, everybody is talking about deregulation and privatization, and the two are closely connected. Deregulation means that the State no longer tells people what to do, so it withdraws from a certain area it has been regulating, and that is a good thing. Privatization means that the State lets others act in its stead. In the case of SNC and Canadian Arsenals Ltd., I think the sale has some advantages for future jobs and there may be a bit of growth as well. However, one thing worries me and I think we should not overlook this possibility. The Government will on occasion be asked to scrutinize export permits for the goods being produced by Canadian Arsenals Ltd., and I am referring to munitions.
I wish to caution those who think that by privatizing Canadian Arsenals we will create many new jobs and foreign markets, that we will be in the export business, and that we will be expanding the sales of Canadian Arsenals. One must
Canadian Arsenals Limited
remember that export permits from the Canadian Government will still be required. We are just saying that Canadians are asking the Government to ensure that we not aid or abet certain groups or governments which take part in subversive activities or war. Even though the company may want to expand into other export fields, it will still have to apply for export permits which will assure Canadians that the company is not dealing with people, organizations, or governments which may be unfriendly to those in the western world who like to preserve democracy.
I only say that in passing because I was told by someone this morning that they saw great potential for expansion of the arsenals business. I do not think we should expect Canada to begin to export arms or war tools. I could probably make a long speech on that subject, Mr. Speaker, but I will avoid it because I know Members would prefer that I speak on the matter of the privatization and sale of Canadian Arsenals Limited under Bill C-87.

Mr. Speaker, I shall, if I may, comment briefly on the work done by my hon. colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), who spoke in Committee and in the House, and who wrote to the Minister-this is a fact-and, practically single-handed, obtained the release of the Arthur Andersen Report. At least for us in the Official Opposition, he was someone on which people could count to strengthen the transaction. I think that the point that he was making was that, while we are selling a corporation, we do not necessarily have to sell its employees with it. We had to see to it that this transaction would be clean, open and absolutely fair for everyone.
It is my sincere opinion that the vigilance shown by the Opposition, led by the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, protected the Government employees who were asking for and who deserved special attention.
Also, Mr. Jean Bergeron, Vice President of the Public Service Alliance of Canada, played a major role in the negotiations; he said the following:
This is a victory for the employees. However, in the future, the Government should ensure that eventual purchasers are aware of the implications before entering blindly into privatization negotiations as they did in the case of Canadian Arsenals Limited.
Mr. Jean Bergeron worked closely with the employees of Canadian Arsenals Limited and did a lot to make the technicalities of this transaction better understood.
I would simply like to remind the House that Mr. Bergeron first used the word "amateurism" and it was not to describe the transaction. I think that this was sufficiently well explained at second reading. Indeed, there have been rather strong comments from people involved in the transaction who had no hesitation in saying that, for some months now, and even since the beginning, the Government has acted amateurishly in this transaction. If the Government had listened to its Privatization Secretariat, it would not have had these problems. Perhaps then the Government would have been able to involve the employees much more than it did. In addition, perhaps it would have remembered that, when such a company is sold, its most important asset, its work force, is also sold and that such a
12600______________________COMMONS DEBATES___________________April 24,1986
Canadian Arsenals Limited
transaction has certain human resources implications that have to be taken into account.
Mr. Speaker, since we are speaking about privatization, as you probably know, I could talk about the privatization of Government services. I am deeply concerned, and I would simply like to remind the House that whenever a corporation is sold, the privatization extends also to the services that the Government has been providing.
For instance, Mr. Speaker, I could mention the teaching of our official languages or language training in the Public Service of Canada. There were budget cuts that resulted in nearly 850 employees losing their jobs, for there are rumours of privatizing that service in the coming year. I can quote from page 6823 of Hansard a question I asked in this House, and in which I suggested it was irresponsible to privatize language training and thereby jeopardize the jobs of 788 employees, 62.6 per cent of whom were women. Moreover, 536 of those 788 employees are members of the teaching personnel and 59 per cent are professional women.
Recently, Mr. Speaker, I also referred to the issue of translators in this House. Part of that essential service has been privatized. Nearly 130 persons were laid off, a majority of whom once again are women. It is hard to accept that Government services should be privatized without cost-benefit studies being made public, whether the service to be privatized will be maintained, whether it will be competent, whether it will be possible for the Canadian people to obtain from this Government an on-going quality of service. This is why we ask the question, and I keep coming back to this, because we always have such "darned difficulty" getting information about the Government.
I asked the Minister in this House to provide us with information on the costs and benefits of privatizing Government services. I am not referring to companies, corporations and so on. I am referring to services, and to this date we do not have many documents. We have had promises. The Minister told me he had handed over everything. I wrote to the Minister on a number of occasions, and I could read you the letters, Mr. Speaker, I still have some of them that were written last February, in which I asked specifically that he answer my question. The question dealt with the tabling of cost-benefit studies on privatization, dated February 11, 1986. I am still waiting for the answer from the Minister. I know the Minister will answer one of these days, but I would like him to do so in the forthcoming days, because it is important for us to know whether the Government has made across-the-board cost-benefit studies.
It was the Minister himself, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) who told me in the House that studies were made with respect to the consequences of privatization. I would now like to read to you, as recorded on page 10246 of Hansard dated January 24, this reply from the Minister:
I will be more than happy to make available to him any studies which we have bearing on the rate of remuneration and on the cost-benefits type of information he is asking that we have at our disposal.
Mr. Speaker, I have yet to receive that information and close to two months have elapsed since it was requested. Now as far as privatization of services is concerned, perhaps the Government could be more forthcoming and helpful in its negotiations if it provided the information we require.
As far as privatizing Canadian Arsenals Limited is concerned, Mr. Speaker, we do not object, as I said earlier, to privatization. We have done our work as Members of this House and we have tried to convince the Government about two things: first, that the deal should guarantee the jobs and the pension fund of the employees. Second, we asked the Government to keep this transaction in mind and not to forget the mistakes they made and to remember that we will be on our toes in the future in case they try to sell out something else.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to conclude my brief remarks by congratulating once again the Hon. Member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell for his contribution to this matter and also thank my colleagues who have taken part in the long debates in the House. I must say that I am glad we have been able to improve this initiative through amendments introduced by the Government and received very positively by the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the decision to privatize Canadian Arsenals is part of the Government's policy and, I guess, ideology. It really has very little to do with any benefit to Canadians generally, or even the people concerned directly. Consequently, although I could spend a considerable amount of time discussing the pros and cons of this privatization, as has been done by others, I think it more important to suggest that, since this privatization has been so incredibly badly handled, perhaps the Government could have learned something. If the Government intends to proceed with its policy and ideology, maybe it has learned something which would make it possible that future privatization projects will be a little more carefully thought out, planned, and consequently function a little more smoothly. I think it is unfortunate that such a great amount of anguish and concern was raised among the employees of Canadian Arsenals by the Government in this process. Some basic openness and understanding in discussing the problems would have eliminated that situation. I want to explore the possibility of putting in place a better system for doing this.
Before doing that, I want to make a few comments on this particular privatization. First, does anyone really think that the privatization of Canadian Arsenals will benefit our economy? The purchaser, SNC Group, is a good employer. They see this as a good business step and they are an acceptable buyer. They are promising to expand the business and increase exports. That company is, to some extent, already in the business of munitions, although not necessarily dependent upon this takeover for expansion. If Canada wants to be listed among the exporters of
munitions, of death, if you will, around the world, then I guess it would be all right to divest ourselves of this operation and encourage a private company to expand its export sales. However, I am not sure that the people of Canada really want to go in that direction. I am not sure that the people of Canada were very unhappy with the idea that at least the production of large calibre munitions was controlled by a company owned and operated by the Government.

speechtext:

speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, on the evening of April 24, 1915, 254 Armenian intellectuals were arrested in Istanbul, never to be seen again. Talaat Pasha, who was Minister of the Interior, said: "I will deal the Armenians such a blow that they will not be able to raise their heads for 50 years". He was the cruel, prophetic architect of the genocide which began 71 years ago today.
Before World War I there were two million Armenians in the Ottoman Empire. After the war there were only 100,000. Canada must help to right this wrong. The facts are clear. A recent United Nations subcommittee's report refers to "The Ottoman Massacre of Armenians". We stand with Mr. Hagopian, Chairman of the Armenian National Committee of Canada, and all Canadians of Armenian heritage, to win this battle of human rights recognition that the genocide did occur.

Mr. Speaker, today we commemorate the seventy-first anniversary of the Armenian massacre. Hundreds of people gathered on Parliament Hill today to recognize what has been stated to be the first great act of genocide in this century. It is time for our Government and other Governments to do something about it.
Many of us will gather this evening at the Baltic dinner to recognize the actions of the Soviet Union against the Baltic republics. We do not expect to have very much influence on the Soviet Union. But when we are dealing with allies in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization we do expect to have some influence. It is time for the Government of Canada to press the Government of Turkey to recognize and acknowledge the atrocity of 1915, and to press that Government to provide redress to the Armenian people.

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT

speechtext:
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mclnnes (Minister of Supply and Services) that Bill C-87, An Act to authorize the divestiture of Canadian Arsenals Limited and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the third time and passed.
Canadian Arsenals Limited

subtopic: CANADIAN ARSENALS LIMITED DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we recessed for lunch, I was attempting to explain some of our concerns about the procedures in this Bill.
I believe we can show that this divestiture is not necessarily in the best interests of the economy of Canada. It is very definitely not in the best interests of the employees of Canadian Arsenals who were concerned about their pensions and job security. Furthermore, since this divestiture would involve a transfer from one labour code to another, they were concerned about not being covered by a bargaining agent during that transfer and that there would be no protection for their collective agreements.
I am disturbed at the Government's lack of effort to attempt to come to a satisfactory agreement with SNC, or at least advise that company what was involved in its purchase of Canadian Arsenals. It is obvious that the Government intended to use its majority to push the Bill through the House without any consideration for its side effects on the employees.
Canadian Arsenals Limited had good labour relations, and I understand that these good relations still exist with the new company. However, the Government was prepared to make the transfer without ensuring that those good labour relations would continue. If the Member from the Liberal Party and I had not held up the Bill and insisted on negotiations with SNC, it is not unreasonable to believe that the employees of Canadian Arsenals would have been prepared to strike as a result of being dealt with unfairly during this takeover period. That is not the kind of company that SNC thought it was purchasing.
Perhaps Members will recall when the employees of Canadian Arsenals demonstrated on the Hill. The fact that they found it necessary to do this is unbelievable in itself. Those demonstrators wore buttons saying that they were an explosive union. The point they were making is that labour unrest is very dangerous in their kind of work and therefore the Government should have ensured that everything was in place before the transfer was made.
This Bill has now reached third reading stage, which means this is the final opportunity to discuss the Bill. Can we expect the Government to take a much more careful approach to privatization in the future? In this particular case every step of the process was sloppy. There was sloppy planning and an arrogant disregard for the people involved. The employees were left out of the negotiations. The whole process was kept secret to the point where everyone involved with it was uncomfortable. I believe that even Members of the Government felt they did not have enough information.
I want to spend a few minutes on the procedure because I think procedure is critical to the concerns of Government with respect to the divestiture of future corporations. Possibly there will be a less disturbing procedure in the future because the

April 24, 1986
Canadian Arsenals Limited
Government has learned something from its unbelievably inept handling of this divestiture.
I would like to put before the House the following procedures which I believe should have been followed. First, when the decision has been made to sell the Government should follow the requirements of Section 99 of the Financial Administration Act and have the Minister table in this House his directive to the corporation. In this particular case the Government did not follow the law of the land and table before this House a directive saying this Company was going to be sold. 1 know the Minister suggested he did not have to do that, but the law says he does. The Minister failed to fulfil those requirements. Had he done so, we would have had a situation where everyone in the House knew the procedures which were to be followed. I think it is typical of the arrogance of the Government that it was unwilling to fulfil the requirements of the laws of the country.
Second, there should be full and complete disclosure of the tendering process and criteria, possibly in tabling the Financial Administration Act directive. The public, the employees and any possible interested purchasers have the right to receive that kind of information.
At the same time the Government should have put before Parliament a Bill-not after they sold the company but before-that would allow it to sell the company which could be discussed within the structure of Parliament. I believe it is very arrogant of the Government to require Parliament to pass a Bill forming the company and then bring a Bill before Parliament suggesting we rubber stamp it because it has already sold the company. A Bill to sell the company should have been passed before the tenders were called. In that Bill should have been placed the kind of information which would have allowed the bidding company to know it would be taking over a certain kind of agreement with respect to the employees, and that it had some responsibility to have a continuum of employee benefits. That was not in the Bill at all, and it was not done in this divestiture until it was forced upon the Government and the purchaser. The purchaser had already made the deal before it knew it had problems with the employee agreement. This, in my opinion, was very inept on the part of the Government.
The Bill should include a price which the Government thinks the corporation is worth, so that when tenders are submitted Parliament can make some decision and approach the situation with some secure knowledge that the corporation was not passed on as part of a patronage deal by the Government. Before the Government asked for tenders it should have established a price range within which it would be acceptable to sell the corporation. The Government should put itself beyond suspicion. It should say: "This is what the corporation is worth. Let Parliament look at that". It should then call for tenders. If it does not get that amount it could sell the corporation later or suggest to Parliament the reasons why it cannot get that price.
The Bill, and possibly the tender papers, should set down the rules as far as the employees are concerned. The tendering criteria must be included in the conditions of sale so that we do not have the same kind of situation we had in this divestiture where, for a period of several months after the actual sale had been completed, negotiations went on between SNC, the Government of Canada and the employees. That is an incredible way of doing business. If the conditions of sale show the contractual and acquired rights of the employees and include the vesting of their pensions and their rights within the Superannuation Act, it could then be maintained in the sale and the purchaser would know what it was getting into.
Finally, available to Parliament before the sale is confirmed should be all of the information with respect to price and the conditions of sale. If possible, they should be made public at that time so that no one could accuse the Government or the Parliament of Canada of allowing a divestiture to go through with the suspicion of patronage. I believe the agreement between the corporation and the Government of Canada should be in the public domain so that everyone could know that the deal was good, and acceptable.
In summary, I have laid down what I think would be an acceptable procedure. First, the required directive should be tabled in the House. The Bill should be brought before the House and passed. By passing the Bill Parliament gives the Government the athority to sell. It could not set the company up without the authority to do so, why should it be able to sell without that authority? The tendering papers should be made public. The Government should then go into negotiations for sale with the conditions passed by Parliament. When the purchaser has been identified and the price agreed upon, the Government should again refer it to committee as it did, at least partially, with de Havilland.
Finally, the agreement should be considered in the public domain which would, of course, be the case if the above course were followed. Before we go ahead with any further divestitures or privatizations we need to establish a procedure which is acceptable to the employees, to Members of the House of Commons and to the Government.

subtopic: PARLIAMENTARY EMPLOYMENT AND STAFF RELATIONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to take part this afternoon in the debate on Bill C-45 to establish a system of labour relations between employer and employees of the Senate and the House of Commons.
This Bill is obviously very important because, for the first time, legislation will recognize a basic right of the workers on Parliament Hill, namely the right to associate and to be represented by the president and officers of their union to defend their interests.
My colleague for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) presented an amendment asking that this Bill not be read now, but in one month from this day. Why do we want this Bill to be read only in one month from now? It is because we want to give an opportunity to the representatives of the employees on Parliament Hill and the employer to agree on provisions which would be acceptable to both parties.
The Bill introduced by the Government does not satisfy the employees of the House of Commons. We have all received a document which clearly states ... If I can put a hand on it, I have a copy of it which I would like to read very quickly. This document, which was sent to all Members of Parliament and Senators and was signed by Mr. Jacques Audette, says the following:
You will soon be asked to vote on Bill C-45 respecting Parliamentary employment and staff relations. As those most closely affected, the employees of Parliament Hill ask you to consider the serious concerns raised by this Bill.
This letter refers to a number of points of which our employees do not really approve, namely:
The questions which were and still are of greatest concern to us are classification, job descriptions, competitions, promotions, transfers and the fear of being laid off or fired. The answer to these questions has always been left to the sole discretion of management and this has resulted in serious cases of abuse. Many of us are incorrectly classified and often have no job description. Many of us have applied in vain for promotions or transfers, because the rules governing the competitions were arbitrarily changed in the middle of the game.
I am still quoting Mr. Audette, Chairman of that local of the Association of Parliamentary employees.
Reading that document, Mr. Speaker, one realizes that Bill C-45 is not unanimously supported. More than that, it has given rise to a number of major objections on the part of employees.
What seems quite important, and I will quote yet another paragraph from that letter:
Under the Canadian Labour Code, it is possible to resolve problems through collective bargaining. However, Bill C-45 would not allow us to deal efficiently with any of the above matters. By not allowing us to negotiate classification or to refer staffing problems to arbitration, you will be maintaining the status quo.
Mr. Audette concludes, and I quote:
And the status quo means lower employee morale and sources of problems for all of us.
You know there have been representations made to the courts and that no later than today, the Federal Appeal Court issued its findings in the case of the House of Commons vs the Canadian Labour Relations Board and the Public Service Alliance of Canada.
April 24, 1986

The judgment was delivered today by Mr. Justice Pratte and I believe it is a major new development that we must now take into account. What is essential in my view is that the motion to delay for one month the reading of this legislation, which was put forward by my colleague for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps), becomes that much more relevant.
It is absolutely vital in my view that, if we are to legislate a new status for employees of the House of Commons, the Senate and the Library, we should have a minimum of employee support and satisfaction.
I think one of the basic questions which the Government was concerned about and which prevented it from drafting legislation that would subject those parliamentary employees to the Canada Labour Code, is that under the Canada Labour Code they would have the right to strike. And I do not think I am being unfair to the Conservative Government when I say that the idea, the possibility that parliamentary employees might some day go on strike has sent such a shiver down our Government friends' backs that they have decided to have parliamentary employees subjected to the Public Service Staff Relations Act rather than to the Canada Labour Code.

As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, unfortunately, the wish not to provide the right to strike probably brought the Government to introduce a Bill which does not meet in its present form the hopes and expectations of Parliamentary employees.

I want to read here a note that has been given to me that I believe is one that could be a happy compromise. Bill C-45 does not allow Hill employees the right to strike, a right they

It is quite clear to me, Mr. Speaker, that the concerns expressed by Mr. Audette, especially about classification, promotion and lay-offs, are points which we cannot take lightly and which deserve our attention. I therefore felt that I had to rise at this time to tell the Government Members that they should, in this first piece of legislation governing Parliamentary employees, show much more trust in these hundred of employees who have been working on the Hill for years faithfully and conscienciously and who have never caused any trouble. No one can say that these employees are trouble makers or that they have provoked many labour conflicts. I think that their past performance is a guarantee for the future and I would like the Government to show them a bit more compassion and understanding. The possibilities for an agreement between the employer and employees of Parliament are obvious. When I was myself Minister of Labour, I invited Parliament to legislate as soon as possible to give to the employees of the House of Commons the union and the legal status that they wished to have, and to do so before the case was referred to the Canada Labour Relations Board. I have to say that both this Government and the previous one took too long to realize that the employees of Parliament had every reason to want to organize and defend themselves better. The previous Government should have introduced a Bill well before this issue was submitted to the Canada Labour Relations Board, and the present Government should have negotiated with the representatives of Parliament employees and introduced a Bill more acceptable than Bill C-45 well before this case had to be heard by the Federal Court and the Appeal Division of the Federal Court.
I especially deplore some aspects of the Bill before us, and I must say that if we could obtain from the Government the assurance that it will introduce the appropriate amendments to give Parliament employees the guaranties they are seeking-I suggest, quite rightfully so-as to classification, job descriptions, promotions, transfers and dismissals, I am sure that on this side of the House, both my colleagues of the Liberal party and the members of the New Democratic Party would be more inclined to proceed quickly with this Bill. But neither the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn) nor the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) have given us clear and definite indications that this Bill could be amended along the lines of the Parliament employees representatives' legitimate claims. As members of the Liberal party, we find that this Bill is not going in the direction we would have given it had we still been in the Government. I can tell you certainly that as a former Minister of Labour, if I were still Minister of Labour, I would make pressing representations to the

President of the Privy Council and the President of the Treasury Board to amend this Bill as soon as possible in a manner consistent with the views and requests of Parliament employees.
I find somewhat surprising, and even a little absurd, that the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight) who certainly has a general responsibility toward all Canadian workers, and especially those he meets daily on Parliament Hill has not come out more strongly on the side of Parliament employees. I ask the Minister of Labour to wake up, read this Bill, read the representations made by representatives of the Public Service Alliance, and especially those of Parliament employees, and then exert pressures on his colleagues to have Bill C-45 properly amended.
But the best thing that we could do at this time, Mr. Speaker, would be to accept the motion moved by my colleague the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps), that this Bill be not now read a second time but that it be read one month hence, in order to reach an agreement negotiated in good faith between the employer and employees on Parliament Hill. I am sure that if we took advantage of that month to sit down, discuss frankly and reach the necessary compromise, we would not have to debate this Bill in the House. Following an agreement between the employer and employees on the Hill, the Government could introduce a Bill that would receive unanimous approval. We in the Liberal Party would be the first to support the Government if it could reach such an agreement after consultation and frank negotiations with employee representatives.
I am therefore asking the House to postpone this debate for one month to give the President of the Privy Council and the President of the Treasury Board a chance to notify the employer forthwith, ask him to sit down with the representatives of our employees and determine once and for all the details of the legal framework that will govern them in the future.

However, the decision of the Appeal Division of the Federal Court only highlights part of the problem. And in my opinion the legal process at this time is in a way an adversary, not a consultation process. If the parties feel that they have to appeal to courts to have their rights recognized, there has to be a lack of communication and understanding somewhere between the parties.
I believe that instead of carrying on with this process of court settlements, it would be a lot better on the part of the employer to say: "Well, we won our case with the Appeal Division of the Federal Court, but that does not mean that our position is stricly adamant". In my view, the very fact that the employer has won should encourage him to be more magnanimous, more flexible, more generous with Parliament Hill workers, to sit down with them and agree to the appropriate trade-offs in Bill C-45, so that everyone can be happy. Then the employer and all the workers of Parliament Hill as well as Government and Opposition Members could unanimously pass an amended bill that would satisfy parties involved.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to join in this debate on Bill C-45 which relates to the question of collective bargaining for the staff of the House of Commons, the Senate and the Library of Parliament.
I note the question before us this afternoon is an amending motion for second reading a month hence-a one month hoist rather than a six-month hoist-but whatever the period of time involved, I want to speak in support of that amending motion because this not a Bill which deserves to become part of the statute law of Canada.
If we are to become concerned about the rights of parliamentary Hill staff and if we want to ensure that they have good working conditions and their lives on the Hill are the kinds of lives our employees should lead, then it seems to me the question becomes quite a fundamental one. This is a question of how we as parliamentarians treat our own, those who work for us here and those who are to be seen around us as we carry on the business of Government and the business of debating the national questions with which we are faced. I think also of those who serve us in our offices and those who provide assistance to us from the Library of Parliament. The question of how we are going to treat these persons who work around us and with us is a question which raises the most fundamental concerns about our own integrity and the honesty with which we handle people's lives.
This Parliament, after all, in years past established in the Statutes the Canada Labour Code provisions governing those workers away from the Hill who are under federal regulation. It was significant that the Canada Labour Code made many advances. It attempted to establish a fine standard for employees across the country in federal undertakings. What could one say, however, about the fact that the Canada Labour Code was not the basis for the relations with employers of members of the Public Service? What could one say when the Government of Canada presumed to impose on workers in federally regulated undertakings a high standard and then accepted a much lower standard in the form of the Public Service Staff Relations Act for the Public Service of the

April 24, 1986
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act
country? Surely there is a kind of hypocrisy involved in such action which could lead the managers of the country, and much more so the workers and their unions, to wonder about the right of a Government through Parliament to impose on these various federal undertakings those standards when the Government of Canada was not ready to maintain the standards for itself.
We find now the question of the representation of workers on the Hill becoming a clear-cut issue when we see the Public Service Alliance pressing the organization of workers and seeking to establish before the Canada Relations Board that the Parliament Hill staff be regarded as a federal undertaking in the sense of bringing to bear the provisions of the Canada Labour Code.
What can we say about the fact that the Government's response to that was a tranposition of the Public Service Staff Relations Act on these employees? In this way their rights to collective bargaining in a number of very important ways is limited. These workers might very well feel that they have their rights provided for when, in fact, in area after vital area they do not have the protection they need. That strikes me as a kind of institutionalizing of hypocrisy of which any Government should be ashamed. I challenge my colleagues across the way to consider this question very seriously. I challenge them to ask themselves whether it is right to demand of employers across the country high standards while in our treatment of those who work for us every day we are prepared to allow all types of abuses to occur.
My friend, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt, during the time allotted for questions and comments reminded the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), and all Members of the House, that abuse of workers on Parliament Hill has been controversial in the last year or more. He pointed out that there has been a certain putting on to the public record suspicions, rumours and allegations which only floated about in the past. Some of the worst abuses refer to suggestions of sexual harassment and charges of favouritism and of nepotism which have become bywords around the House of Commons.
My friend from Nickel Belt was quite justified in pointing out that, after having governed for the better part of two decades, the Liberals brought in the Canada Labour Code but settled for the Public Service Staff Relations Act for the Public Service. They did not really provide any reform or protection for workers on the Hill.
It is worth taking a look at what some of the results of this failure to legislate have been. I note, among a number of cases, that our employees have put forward such instances as the following. In a technical service a senior position became vacant. Several employees inquired when a competition would be held to fill the position. There was no competition. Then the husband of a manager in another department of the same service was brought in to fill the post-on a temporary basis, of course. Several months later a competition was announced.
The now-experienced husband was hired permanently and the attempt of employees in the service to appeal this particular piece of institutional nepotism was denied.
The next example I have occurred in a support service where several employees held working supervisor positions on an acting basis. They had been in these acting positions for seven, five, three and two years respectively. They were informed that they would be downgraded four levels. Their salaries dropped from $21,000 per year to $17,000 per year. During the same period of time new working supervisors were hired without any competition having been carried out. When the former acting supervisors attempted to appeal internally, their appeals were denied. This is an abuse of workers, particularly when one contemplates someone left in a working supervisor position on an acting basis for seven years. Surely, that in itself is outrageous.
The next example I have to put forward occurred in the printing branch. Staff on the Hill are well aware that there is a hiring freeze in effect. In fact, some employees in this branch had been transferred out to other government Departments or offered incentives to take early retirement. However, new casual staff were hired in the printing branch and at least in one case there is a close family link to the senior management of the branch. Again, one sees nepotism as a partial justification for the abuse of experienced employees in the branch.
The next case I have deals with employees in a technical service who were required to attend training courses on their days off, on weekends, without any pay. When they protested this abuse of their free time, they were told that the training courses were mandatory and they had no choice but to take them. That type of arbitrary behaviour from those in supervisory positions strikes me as an outrageous example of what can happen when workers do not have the rights which should apply to them as employees.
I would like to point out one last example of the type of abuses which have occurred. There was in place an employee assistance program which was established for employees of the House of Commons as a type of safety-valve. Given the examples I have just presented, I am sure a safety-valve was more than necessary. This was a means of having personal problems dealt with in confidence by a qualified counsellor. Early in 1985 the counsellor in charge of this employee assistance program was fired, the position was abolished and the program responsibility was turned over to the nurses. An appeal to the Speaker asking that the position be re-established was denied. Petitions signed by no fewer than 1,500 employees were ignored by the Speaker's office and by Parliament Hill administration. I note that there was a total of about 3,600 staff members on the Hill, at least in 1984-85, and 1,500 is not very far from one-half of the total number of employees.
Recognizing the types of abuses which have occurred and those which will occur when managers cannot be brought to book and when workers cannot carry through on appeals, I wish to take a look at some provisions of the Bill which is before us. The amendment to the motion suggests that it be
April 24, 1986

dealt with in one month hence, which might even kill the Bill. I note that there are a number of shortcomings which deal with the fact that classification cannot be dealt with under the proposed legislation. I have already noted some of the appointment weaknesses which are found in the Bill. However, Clause 5(3) would prevent any negotiation with respect to problems related to classification. There is no provision for the employees' union to negotiate job descriptions, or for an opportunity to negotiate the assignment of pay levels, or for the possibility of negotiations dealing with the evaluation of duties. This is, of course, a failure of the legislation to deal with one very large complex of grievances, a system which has evolved over the years, as far as job classification is concerned, which has been an enormous source of dissatisfaction for employees. Many employees do not even have job descriptions. Those who do find that they are often out of date and that they can be arbitrarily changed in an environment which we all realize has seen a good deal of change over the last years. The result is obviously a great deal of employee frustration, insecurity and poor morale.
Similarly, when it comes to the question of staffing, we find that Clause 55(2) prohibits the possibility of bringing the issues of job appointments, job appraisals, promotions, demotions, transfers, lay-offs or releases to third-party arbitration. There is no possibility of having these equally contentious matters, at least in their potential, dealt with to a resolution which will be genuinely impartial through third-party arbitration. These are the types of issues which have been central to the drive by parliamentary employees to gain bargaining rights.
Parliament Hill has had a history of staffing decisions coloured by political influence, favouritism, nepotism, and administrative incompetence. The Government has no desire to change that fundamentally. I should like to add to these areas of weakness. The lack of a grievance procedure to deal with a great diversity of problems which can arise between our managers and our employees is surely the most fundamental weakness in the Act. If there is one thing collective bargaining should provide, it should provide a basis for resolving conflicts under the rule of law through a grievance procedure and, if necessary, into third party arbitration.
I have emphasized the importance of applying sound principles of collective bargaining to Hill employees. I have been critical of the present Government and of previous Governments for hypocrisy in legislating well for others but failing to apply the same principles to their own actions. In this kind of context it is quite appropriate for others to say something like: "Put up or shut up. You state these principles, but what will you do about them yourselves?" I say with some pride that the New Democratic Party caucus has been true to the principles which helped create the movement of the CCF and the NDP. We have been faithful to our employees.
Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act
Our power as Members of Parliament employing them has been constrained by the conditions which the Government imposes upon us through the Board of Internal Economy in particular. However, New Democratic Party members have in fact gone the route of collective bargaining with our employees. I say with pride that we have done so as far back as 1977. Obviously it was done by my predecessors such as the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) and others who made the decision at that time to negotiate with a parliamentary association of support staff comprised of our assistants on the Hill, assistants who were in fact, in full legal fact, some of the Hill employees about whom I am talking. In effect we created a bargaining unit of support staff, and our caucus members took on the responsibility of being employers and regarded themselves explicitly as employers. That process has continued.
There have been several rounds of negotiations and elaboration of the collective agreement. As is inevitable in these circumstances, we have found that difficulties can arise at times, that difficult questions must be answered, that collective agreements need to be refined, and so on.
Since becoming a Member of Parliament in 1984 I have had some involvement with those matters. However, in all honesty and honour, I say on behalf of my colleagues and myself that we accepted the principle that collective bargaining should apply to our relations with our staff. We knew that we could not control what they earned. We knew that there were various constraints upon us as employers which put us in a difficult position at times, a position our staff members had to recognize when they dealt with us. However, where we could, we provided for them in every area.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Hon. Member. I followed his remarks attentively, and I think he spoke sincerely. Today's judgment in the Federal Court came as a surprise to many of us. Nevertheless, we will have to await the reaction of the unions to see whether they will go to the Supreme Court of Canada with the matter.
My question concerns the right to strike of Hill employees. The Hon. Member knows that in the Bill before us the right to strike is not given to employees on the Hill. He also knows that employees through their unions have held fast to the right to withdraw services if they feel there is a conflict between the employer and the employees, and they want to make it public. We all know the origin of strikes; it was to inform the population at large that indeed there was a conflict between the employer and the employees. He also knows that our employees have referred to meaningful arbitration. I do not know whether I should expand upon what is meant by meaningful arbitration, but it would include classification standards, promotions, demotions, and all other matters concerning nominations and appointments.
I am referring to the general subject matter of arbitrating conflicts and disagreements, and I know that our employees may be flexible on this matter. My question is not an academic one; I want to know where the Hon. Member stands. What would he do if we gave the right to strike to employees on the Hill? If indeed a picket was set up to protest, object, or inform the public of a conflict, would the Hon. Member cross that picket line?

Mr. Speaker, that is the second such answer I have had from that Party. Other members of that Party have said that given a crisis situation where Parliament had to sit and they had to represent their constituents, they would inform the striking employees and come here to do their duty as they were elected to do. The Hon. Member said that he would not cross a picket line; I accept that as an honest answer. I simply say to him that there is disagreement within his own Party. Perhaps they should have a meeting of the minds in the NDP to find out what they would do in the event that the right to strike was given to our employees. They are always preaching about what we should have done and did not do. However, when they are called upon to make a decision, sometimes they are divided, as they are on this issue. I would like them to put their heads together and come up with a definition of what is a designated employee and a definition of what is an essential service.
The point at hand is whether Parliament is an essential service. If it is, then it must sit and do what it was elected to
do, that is, pass laws. If we read today's judgment of the Federal Court, we find that the House of Commons is not an ordinary place. It is the place where constitutionally we must pass laws. If it is our obligation to be in the House to vote, then the Hon. Member had better tell his constituents what he stands for and why he was elected to the House. If the picket line stops him from doing his duty, then the Member will have to tell us why he cannot take his place in the House and do the things he should be doing that he was elected by his constituents to do.

Private Members' Business

On the same point of order, Mr. Speaker, I would also like to seek your advice on this question. Member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) which has recommended that some items be votable. But that committee wondered what would happen if a motion were called without its sponsor being present. Mr. Speaker, it's a rather important problem which I submit to you and I should like you to enlighten us, because it would mean that an Hon. Member, let us say our colleague the Hon. Members to have a completely new schedule? That's the problem I wanted to point out to you.

Private Members ' Business

Mr. Speaker, I rise on this point of order. I assume the decision will be made by the Speaker as opposed to the House Leaders. We are discussing the sequence of speakers during Private Members' Hour.
